items.why_lost: In the LDR design questions a wrong symbol or an unjustified resistor value keeps you off the top mark, and a wrongly placed voltmeter drops you to Level 1.
items.what_scores: Standard LDR symbol, voltmeter correctly across the fixed resistor (or as specified), justified resistor value with calculated outputs for bright and dark conditions.

items.looks_right: Drawing the emerging ray parallel to the incident ray when the second medium differs, curving rays freehand, or showing no bend.
items.why_lost: Rays must bend the correct way at each boundary, be straight by eye, and not be parallel to the incoming ray when the media differ; TIR rays must reflect at the right angles.
items.what_scores: Use a ruler; bend towards the normal into a denser medium and away into a less dense one; for TIR show reflection at the correct boundary with equal angles.

items.looks_right: Labelling the angles of incidence and refraction between the ray and the surface of the block.
items.why_lost: Angles must be measured from a normal drawn at 90 degrees to the surface at the point of incidence.
items.what_scores: Draw the normal at 90 degrees at P, label i between normal and incident ray and r between normal and refracted ray.
items.severity: lose all marks for that part

items.looks_right: Drawing roughly the right shape but leaving the triangle open or arrows chasing in the wrong sense.
items.why_lost: Separate marks for the scaled weight line, a closed triangle and correct arrow directions with a measured value in tolerance.
items.what_scores: Draw the weight to the stated scale, add the other forces head-to-tail to close the triangle, arrow each side, then measure length and angle.

items.topic: Locating centre of gravity of a triangle
items.looks_right: Drawing a single line from an apex and guessing where C is.
items.why_lost: One line gets only the first mark; the position needs at least two medians crossing, and the value must be the single distance (not a range).
items.what_scores: Draw at least two lines from the midpoint of a side to the opposite apex, label their intersection C and measure its distance.

items.looks_right: Drawing one cycle, or wrong amplitude.
items.why_lost: Marks for the correct amplitude and for a sinusoidal shape with the right period over at least two waves; peaks and troughs are checked.
items.what_scores: Draw at least two full sinusoidal cycles with the specified amplitude and wavelength.

items.looks_right: Labelling the downward arrow 'gravity', or writing 24 N on both the push and the friction arrows.
items.why_lost: 'Gravity' as a label is ignored; the numerical value may be given to T or friction but not both; the reaction arrow must match the weight arrow in length.
items.what_scores: Label weight (W, mg or force due to gravity) and normal reaction (R/N) with equal lengths; horizontal push and friction in opposite directions.

items.topic: Nodes and antinodes in a closed pipe
items.looks_right: Drawing the stationary-wave envelope correctly but not labelling it.
items.why_lost: A separate mark is for labelling N and A correctly.
items.what_scores: Node at the closed end, antinode at the open end, both labelled.

items.looks_right: Getting the number right and leaving out the unit (or giving 'A s' style units not asked for).
items.why_lost: Several parts have an independent B1 just for the unit; the number alone loses it.
items.what_scores: Always write the unit: C for charge, ohm m for resistivity, N s or kg m s^-1 for impulse, Pa s (or kg m^-1 s^-1) for viscosity.

items.topic: Unit must match the power of ten
items.looks_right: Working out a force constant from a graph in cm and writing N m^-1 without converting, or giving a radius in m when km was used.
items.why_lost: The scheme insists the unit carries the correct power of ten (e.g. 0.55 N cm^-1 or 55 N m^-1, but not 0.55 N m^-1); one answer 'must be km'.
items.what_scores: Check the unit you write matches the scale of your number.

items.looks_right: Using ms, kHz, g, mm, cm^3 or THz values without converting (e.g. 0.67 instead of 670 Hz, 2.7e6 kg m^-3, 60 instead of 0.060).
items.why_lost: A POT error loses the answer mark; the scheme often notes 'the right digits to any power of ten scores one mark'.
items.what_scores: Convert every prefix to SI before substituting, and sanity-check the size of the answer.

items.topic: Show that base units of the volt
items.looks_right: Jumping straight to kg m^2 A^-1 s^-3.
items.why_lost: The final line is A0; marks are for writing C = A s, J = N m = kg m^2 s^-2 and a clear division.
items.what_scores: Show each base-unit substitution explicitly.
items.severity: lose all marks for that part

items.topic: Answers that must be to a stated number of sig figs
items.looks_right: Giving 2738 kg m^-3 when '2 sf' was demanded, 1.3 or 1.4 for a refractive index, 0.06 for 0.060, or 2.5e-4 m when 3 sf was required.
items.why_lost: These are explicit exceptions to the general sf rule: the wrong number of sf loses the answer mark (sometimes leaving 1 mark).
items.what_scores: When the question or scheme specifies sf, give exactly that many (e.g. 2.7e3, 0.060, 2.51e-4, 1.16 km, 1.36).

items.looks_right: Writing 0.5 m s^-2, 2 (gradient), 60 J or 0.1 J.
items.why_lost: Refused in these parts as too few significant figures (or because the 1 sf value is outside the range).

items.looks_right: Ending a show-that on exactly the given rounded value (e.g. 0.64 s, 336 m s^-1 to 2 sf).
items.why_lost: Matching the given value to the same sf does not show it; one scheme caps a 2 sf solution at 3 of 4 marks.
items.what_scores: Quote the unrounded or one-more-sf result before rounding (e.g. 0.642, 0.6296).

items.looks_right: Writing '10%' or '4%' with no working.
items.why_lost: A bald rounded value is refused; the rounded value is only allowed with evidence of working.
items.what_scores: Show each fractional uncertainty, the sum, and the result.

items.looks_right: Choosing a ruler to measure a ball/wire diameter or a thickness.
items.why_lost: Ruler is refused; one scheme also refused the vague 'vernier scale'.
items.what_scores: Micrometer (screw gauge) or (vernier) calipers.
items.severity: lose all marks for that part

items.looks_right: Repeating the reading several times at the same place.
items.why_lost: The mark needs repeats in different directions / positions (along the wire, different orientations) and averaging.
items.what_scores: Repeat at several positions/orientations and take the mean.

items.looks_right: Using a ruler or micrometer across one fringe.
items.why_lost: Both instruments are explicitly refused here.
items.what_scores: Calipers (or travelling microscope) across n fringes, then divide by n.

items.looks_right: Using a stopwatch, or 'light gates' with no mention of a timer.
items.why_lost: Stopwatch is refused; light gates without the timing system earn just one mark; one six-marker ignores light gates and video altogether.
items.what_scores: Electronic timer started by switching off an electromagnet and stopped by a trapdoor (or two light gates to a timer); height with a metre rule, allowing for the ball's diameter.

items.looks_right: Choosing the most precise meter without checking it can read the value.
items.why_lost: Range must cover the reading and resolution must suit it.
items.what_scores: Pick the meter whose range includes the value with the finest resolution.

items.looks_right: Writing f = 1/T without saying how T is found.
items.why_lost: Only one mark if T is not defined.
items.what_scores: Period = number of divisions x timebase setting; then f = 1/T.

items.looks_right: Quoting the gradient's percentage uncertainty for g even though g = 2/gradient^2, or using a rounded 10% with no line.
items.why_lost: Percentage uncertainty in the final quantity equals that of the gradient only if they are directly or inversely proportional; for a squared relationship it doubles.
items.what_scores: Gradient of best and worst lines, absolute difference, percentage of best gradient, then apply the power in the relationship.

items.looks_right: Calling the straight-line component a 'metallic conductor'.
items.why_lost: Refused - the expected answer is a (fixed, ohmic) resistor; a filament lamp (or ptc thermistor/heater) for the curve.
items.what_scores: Name the component: resistor for straight line through origin; filament lamp for the S-shaped curve.

items.looks_right: A detailed method with no analysis, or analysis with no method.
items.why_lost: Level 3 needs procedure AND measurements AND analysis; missing one caps you at Level 2.
items.what_scores: Cover all three: what you do, what you measure with which instrument, and how you process (equation, graph, gradient meaning).

items.looks_right: Describing apparatus in words only.
items.why_lost: The top-level descriptors in several schemes specify a (clear, labelled) diagram.
items.what_scores: Include a labelled diagram of the set-up.

items.looks_right: Writing 'be careful' or 'wear safety equipment'.
items.why_lost: The indicative content lists specific precautions (goggles / screen for snapping wire, tray or gloves for liquids, cushion or sand bag under falling masses, ear defenders, insulated connections for high voltage, switching off to avoid heating).
items.what_scores: Name a precaution specific to the hazard in the experiment.

items.looks_right: Finding v, g or h correctly from the gradient but skipping the percentage uncertainty the question also asked for.
items.why_lost: The Level 3 descriptor includes determining the percentage uncertainty; without it the answer sits at Level 2 at best.
items.what_scores: Draw the worst acceptable line, find its gradient, the absolute uncertainty (difference from best gradient), the percentage uncertainty, and transfer it to the final quantity (applying any power).

items.looks_right: A clear qualitative story (e.g. 'higher p.d., faster electrons, shorter wavelength') with no equations or numbers.
items.why_lost: Where the question gives data or asks for a comparison/determination, the top level requires a quantitative treatment; a purely qualitative answer is capped.
items.what_scores: Include the numbers: e.g. lambda proportional to 1/sqrt V, path differences, momentum/KE values, de Broglie wavelength of the car.

items.looks_right: Explaining observations well but not giving evidence for photons (or defining terms but not comparing materials).
items.why_lost: Two-part questions put a one-part answer at Level 2 maximum.
items.what_scores: Address both parts explicitly.

items.looks_right: Plotting the raw variables (v against r) when the relationship is squared.
items.why_lost: The analysis marks are for a linearised graph with gradient meaning.
items.what_scores: Plot the graph that is straight through the origin (v vs r^2, x vs 1/f, 1/v^2 vs M, V vs 1/lambda) and state what the gradient equals.

items.looks_right: Timing a falling ball without checking terminal velocity, or starting the resonance search from a random frequency.
items.why_lost: Indicative content credits specific control steps.
items.what_scores: Check terminal velocity (equal times for equal distances), start from low frequency for the fundamental, shield LED to judge switch-on, D much larger than a.

items.looks_right: Explaining maxima and minima by superposition but claiming the minima should be zero, and not using the data.
items.why_lost: Indicative content notes minima are not zero because the reflected path is longer (unequal amplitudes); L3 also needs path differences calculated (Pythagoras) to get the wavelength.
items.what_scores: Explain superposition of coherent waves, path difference changing by lambda/2 between max and min, why minima are not zero, then compute path differences and the wavelength.

items.looks_right: Hitting the right science points in a jumbled order with contradictions or unsupported statements.
items.why_lost: The science content decides the level; the communication statement (clear, logically structured, relevant and substantiated) decides whether you get the higher or lower mark in that level - so a disorganised L3 answer gets 5 not 6.
items.what_scores: Structure the answer (e.g. method -> measurements -> analysis), link each claim to evidence/data, and avoid irrelevant material.

items.looks_right: Using your (wrong) earlier answer correctly in a later part and expecting error-carried-forward credit.
items.why_lost: Several parts explicitly exclude ECF (e.g. wavelength in glass from a wrong speed, braking force from a wrong time, a ray from a wrong critical angle, a harmonic from a wrong diagram); ECF is also never given for wrong physics (XP).
items.what_scores: Double-check values that feed later parts; re-derive from the data where you can.
items.severity: lose all marks for that part

items.looks_right: Getting one of two required values right (e.g. force and time read from a graph, or the two charge carriers).
items.why_lost: Some single marks need both values (no tolerance for graph reads in one case), and one needed the two speeds in the stated order.
items.what_scores: Give every value requested, in the order asked, in the table or answer space provided.
items.severity: lose all marks for that part

items.looks_right: Saying electrons diffract 'because they are small' or just 'they show rings'.
items.why_lost: Credit is for the wavelength condition and the source of the rings.
items.what_scores: De Broglie wavelength (h/p) is comparable to the atomic spacing in graphite; rings because the graphite is polycrystalline / atoms irregularly arranged so diffraction occurs in all directions; bright rings are maxima.

items.topic: Reaction time vs braking changes on a v-t graph
items.looks_right: Saying a tired driver makes the sloping (braking) section change, or that harder braking lengthens the flat section.
items.why_lost: Reaction time only lengthens the horizontal section; braking deceleration only changes the slope; tired-driver braking-force ideas are ignored.
items.what_scores: Reaction time -> longer horizontal section, sloping line unchanged; greater deceleration -> steeper slope, horizontal unchanged.

items.looks_right: Saying intensity halves so the amplitude halves.
items.why_lost: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
items.what_scores: State I proportional to A^2; a quarter of the intensity means half the amplitude (and use it numerically, e.g. ratio 9 for amplitude ratio 3).

items.looks_right: Drawing the arrow in the direction electrons move.
items.why_lost: Conventional current is from positive to negative terminal (opposite to electron flow).
items.what_scores: Arrow from + to - through the external circuit; ions: positive carriers move towards the negative terminal.

items.looks_right: Saying braking would not be constant 'because of wind' or 'because of hills'.
items.why_lost: Wind, turns and gradients are ignored.
items.what_scores: Acceleration is not constant (curved line); braking is applied and released gradually for passenger comfort; resistive forces change with speed.

items.looks_right: Giving a phase difference in wavelengths or leaving 2.25 lambda as the answer.
items.why_lost: Phase difference must be an angle (rad); allowed forms include pi/2, 9pi/2 etc. for 2.25 lambda.
items.what_scores: Phase difference = (path difference / lambda) x 2 pi in radians (or degrees), and say destructive when it is an odd multiple of pi.

items.topic: Power against gravity on a slope
items.looks_right: Using the full weight x distance along the slope for the work done.
items.why_lost: Only the component along the slope (or the vertical height) counts; sin/cos confusion gives one mark.
items.what_scores: Work = mg x distance x sin(slope angle) (equivalently cos of the complement); power = force x velocity including friction.

items.looks_right: Writing P = Fv from memory.
items.why_lost: A derivation needs the starting definitions and algebraic steps.
items.what_scores: Start from P = W/t and W = Fx, then P = Fx/t = Fv.
items.severity: lose all marks for that part

leniencies.detail: The sign of a deceleration, force, momentum change or resultant displacement is ignored; magnitude is enough.
Some parts explicitly allow a 1 s.f. answer without the SF penalty (e.g. 4.0 deceleration as 4, 0.3 W, 4 x 10^-19 J, 2 m/s, 8 ohm, ratio 1, 4 mats, 8 x 10^3 kg/m^3, 30 N m, uncertainties to 1 s.f.).
Giving more s.f. than justified is never penalised (unless the question demands a set number).
'Speed' is accepted for 'velocity' when describing motion from an s-t graph.

leniencies.topic: Interference vs superposition in stationary waves
leniencies.detail: 'Interference' accepted in place of 'superposition' for stationary wave formation.
g = 9.8 m s^-2 accepted as well as 9.81; g = 10 allowed where it gives the same 2 s.f. answer.
Using the rounded given value (e.g. 9 x 10^6 m/s, 90 000 N/m, 3.4 N) in the next part still earns full credit.
Misuse of 'accuracy' and 'precision' was ignored in the mu experiment as long as the procedure was sensible.
Missing graph label Y ignored; triangle of forces orientation ignored; ray directions and extra reflected rays ignored; no labelling of rays/normal needed.
Force arrows may be drawn anywhere on the diagram if directions are correct.
Read-offs and gradients accepted within stated ranges (e.g. gradient 15.5-16.5, 160-180 Hz m, 1.40-1.60, h 6.4-7.4 x 10^-34; times 0.30-0.40 s).
Correct scale drawing accepted for full marks within tolerance (4.5 +/- 0.1 N; 5.4-5.6 cm leading to 7.1 +/- 0.2 m/s).
Any correct method (sine/cosine rule, components, KE route, potential divider, suvat variants) earns full marks; 'any subject' for equations.
The same POT error in a value (0.54 mm^2) is not penalised again in a later part.
Powers of ten and units ignored in a qualitative resistance justification; POT errors ignored in supporting calculations.
A value of k or g written on the answer line next to the uncertainty is ignored.
Energy lost, drag, coherence, thermal energy to surroundings, 'waves don't move', references to frequency/threshold in de Broglie questions are ignored rather than penalised.
'Photoelectron' accepted for electron; loose 'electrons and photons' plural given benefit of doubt.
For the N3 partner of weight, 'planet' or 'ground' was allowed.
sin^2-shaped intensity curve accepted (if positions correct).
An incorrect value for the constant phase difference is ignored.
Rounded intermediate values (e.g. 12.1 N, 5.6 x 10^17) are accepted.
ECF allowed for an incorrect variable-resistor symbol in the internal resistance circuit; battery symbol for cell allowed.
'Extension' accepted for 'compression'; W = mg route allowed.
Adding that coherent waves have the same frequency or wavelength is ignored - it does not cost you, but it does not score either; only 'constant phase difference/relationship' scores.
The sign of a deceleration, braking force or momentum read-off is ignored (or a negative value is allowed) in these parts.

leniencies.topic: Powers of ten in method marks
leniencies.detail: Power-of-ten slips are ignored for the method/intermediate marks (and for gradient values) in these parts; only the final answer is affected, or not at all.

leniencies.topic: Sig figs in percentage uncertainties and gradients
leniencies.detail: Significant figures are explicitly not penalised for percentage uncertainties, gradients read from graphs, and energy from counting squares.
In these parts a 1 sf answer is explicitly accepted (usually because the data or the estimate justify it, or with correct working).
For an estimate (e.g. mass of an adult) or where the effect is negligible, g = 10 m s^-2 is allowed.

Answers that differ slightly because you used a rounded intermediate value (e.g. 16.9 vs 17, 1.6 V vs 1.5 V, 194 000 vs 190 000 J, 458.6 vs 457.8 N) are allowed; rounding in the final step is ignored in one case.
Instead of adding percentage uncertainties you may calculate the maximum and minimum value of the quantity; this is accepted for full marks.
From 2022 the schemes state a general rule: when substituting into an equation any subject is allowed unless the guidance says otherwise (several earlier parts say the same, e.g. resistivity).
Units are ignored for some gradient values, strain, and values entered in a table.
kg s^-2 is accepted for a force constant; N s or kg m s^-1 for impulse; kg m^-1 s^-1, N s m^-2 or Pa s for viscosity; pence or pounds for cost.
'Equal to' is accepted for 'proportional to'; mention of direction is ignored; F = delta p / delta t with symbols defined is fine.
'Torque' is accepted for moment and 'total clockwise = total anticlockwise' / 'total up = total down' for the sums being zero.
'Acceleration is zero' is accepted instead of 'velocity is constant'.
'Travel at the speed of light' is accepted for travelling at 3e8 m s^-1 in a vacuum.
'Work per coulomb' or 'joule per coulomb' is allowed here because a full definition was not required; 'energy transferred' may replace 'work done'.
'Minimum frequency to overcome the work function' is accepted, and 'electrons' or 'photoelectrons' both fine.
Arguing the other way round (ORA) - e.g. what the photon model can explain, or carbon having a smaller n than copper - earns the same marks.
For the conducting-putty diameter a ruler was allowed (unlike the ball/wire diameter questions, where it was refused).
Mentioning radius in the instrument answer is ignored; 'places/points/positions' are all fine for 'directions'.
Arrows on the glass graph, extra circuit components (e.g. a rheostat), other lines on ray diagrams and line lengths in a part assessed later are ignored.
A correct frequency written in the answer space rather than the table is accepted.
Energy methods instead of suvat, other area-splitting methods, a sketch instead of words, or trig instead of Pythagoras are all accepted.
'Speed of approach equals speed of separation' is accepted as the test for an elastic collision.
'Closed system' is accepted for 'no external force' in conservation of momentum.
For the curved I-V characteristic, a ptc thermistor or heater element is also accepted.
Mentioning the ball heating up, a tired driver's braking force, wind or gradients does not lose marks - it is simply ignored.
Readings within half a small square (or within a grid square for an intercept), and gradient values within stated ranges, are all accepted.
A travelling microscope is accepted as an alternative to calipers for fringe separation.
Writing 0 instead of 0.0 for the first reading is allowed (but not 1 for 1.0).

general: Significant figures: if data are to 2 s.f., any answer of 2 or more s.f. is accepted; more s.f. than justified is never penalised; fewer than 2 s.f. is penalised once only in the whole paper (some parts waive it, and some demand exactly 2 s.f.).

ECF: within a question, arithmetic errors (AE), transcription/misreading errors (TE) and power-of-ten/prefix errors (POT) lose only the mark where they happen; later marks follow through. Wrong physics or an incorrect equation (XP) gets no ECF, even if it gives the right number.
Show-that questions: the final printed value carries no mark (A0); you are marked on working and must give a value to more s.f. than the given one.

Mark types: B marks must be explicitly seen; M marks must be seen and gate the A marks; C marks can be implied by later correct working (so a correct answer with sparse working can still score), but B and M marks cannot be implied.
Contradictions (CON): if a response contradicts itself, the mark is lost even if one part is correct.
MCQ: if two letters are given for a single-answer question, no mark is awarded even if one is correct.
Crossed-out work: if a clear alternative is given, the crossed-out version is not marked; if not, it may be marked if legible.
List questions: only the required number of responses is marked, left to right, line by line - extra responses can't rescue you and wrong first responses use up the slots.
Longer answers: if two separate attempts are left, only the first is marked.
Substitution: unless stated otherwise, an equation may be written with any subject.
Underlined words are essential; bracketed words are optional; '/' separates alternatives; AW = alternative wording; ORA = reverse argument accepted.
g = 10 instead of 9.81 is penalised (first use) where it changes the 2 s.f. answer.
Annotation '^' (omission) means the answer is not wrong but not enough - typical of near-miss explanations.

Mark types: B marks are independent but must be seen; M (method) marks must be seen and the dependent A marks are lost without them; C marks can be implied by correct later working (so a correct answer usually earns them); A marks are for the final accurate answer.

In 'show that' questions the final given value carries no mark (A0); all credit is for visible method, so every substitution (with correct powers of ten) must be written down and the result should be quoted to more significant figures than the value given.

Significant figures: if data are given to 2 sf, any answer to 2 or more sf is accepted; extra sf are never penalised; an answer to fewer than 2 sf is penalised once only in the whole paper - unless the guidance for a part sets a specific sf requirement, in which case that part's rule applies.

Error carried forward is given within a question for arithmetic (AE), transcription (TE) and power-of-ten (POT) errors - you lose the mark where the error occurs and can then score the rest - but never for wrong physics (XP). Using an incorrect equation counts as XP even if it happens to give the right number.
Contradictions (CON): if you write two conflicting statements in the same response you get no mark for that point, even if one of them is correct.
Omission (^): an answer can be not wrong but not enough - it gets no credit until the missing detail is present.
Words in brackets in the scheme are not essential; underlined words must appear; '/' separates alternatives; AW means alternative wording is fine; ORA means the reverse argument is fine.
Crossed-out work is not marked if you give an alternative; if you cross out without replacing it, it may still be marked.

List-style questions ('any two from'): only the requested number of responses is marked, left to right and line by line - extra responses are not marked and a wrong first answer cannot be rescued by a correct third.
If you give two separate responses to a question needing one developed answer and do not cross one out, only the first is marked.
Writing anything not worthy of credit scores 0; copying out the question earns nothing.

Level of response (6-mark) questions: the examiner reads the whole answer, chooses the level that best fits the science content, then awards the higher mark only if the communication statement (clear, logically structured, relevant, substantiated line of reasoning) is fully met; otherwise the lower mark.

Level descriptors for practical six-markers typically require all strands (e.g. procedure, measurements, analysis; or description plus quantitative determination); missing a strand usually caps you at Level 2 regardless of quality elsewhere.
From 2022 onwards: when substituting into an equation any subject is allowed unless the guidance says otherwise - but some parts explicitly say the asked quantity must be the subject.
Benefit of doubt (BOD) is given only where 'sufficient work' is shown, so showing working protects you when the final answer is borderline.
Examiners are told to credit unexpected but correct approaches fairly, so a valid alternative method scores full marks.

The Paper 2 front matter has no special rule for the answer line versus the working; in practice many schemes give partial credit for identified slips (e.g. 'right digits, wrong power of ten scores one mark'), which only works if the working is visible.
